---
title: "Getting going in your language"
subtitle: "Colab first, your own machine when you're ready"
---

A few recommendations, if you want them. The honest headline: **you can do this entire course in Google Colab** — nothing to install, works on any machine including a locked-down Chromebook, and it's where the lessons and activities assume you are. Start there; most of you can *stay* there.

But at some point — the design project is a natural moment — running Python on your own machine starts paying off: your files live where you can see them, nothing depends on a wifi connection, and you get a real editor. This page is for that moment. MATLAB has some special steps because we have a license through the school, though overall its installation is probably the easiest of everything here.

::: {.callout-important}
I considered giving NO instructions for installing Python, because local setups require some care and occasional maintenance during the semester — and I want you willing and able to handle that yourselves. (Chasing down an installation problem is excellent training for this course's whole philosophy.) But I relented. Recommendations below — and you will need to do a bit of work from the command line. If you flat-out do not want to do command-line stuff, stay in Colab or go with MATLAB. But for what it's worth: it makes me feel powerful to do command-line stuff.
:::

## Level 0: Google Colab (where everyone starts)

Go to [colab.research.google.com](https://colab.research.google.com), sign in with your university Google account, click **New notebook**. That's the entire installation. Python runs on Google's computers; NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are pre-installed; your notebooks live in your Google Drive. The one thing to learn early is file handling — where an uploaded CSV goes and why it vanishes when the session ends — which is what Base Camp's BC1 session covers.

## Level 1: Python on your machine

There are multiple avenues here, and if you are confident enough to find your own way (e.g., with pip and venv), I believe in you.

My recommendation is to [install **miniconda**](https://www.anaconda.com/docs/getting-started/miniconda/install) — NOT the full Anaconda, which you can find nearby if you really want to, but I'm not linking it. Anaconda is attractive: everything you'd ever need in one install. Also a lot you'll never need, plus a sluggish navigator that insists on cross-checking every package each time you update. I grew to hate it and "downgraded" to miniconda: no navigator, way fewer packages, no regrets.

For the editor, I recommend [**VS Code**](https://code.visualstudio.com) — it supports Jupyter notebooks (so your Colab habits transfer directly), has an integrated terminal, and its GitHub integration will matter to anyone who takes the version-control Side Quest. Install VS Code, then its *Python* and *Jupyter* extensions (VS Code will offer them the first time you open a `.py` or `.ipynb` file).

### Package management

Miniconda starts with essentially no packages, so you'll install what you need from the command line. **NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas** cover this course; [this page has the instructions](https://www.anaconda.com/docs/getting-started/working-with-conda/packages/install-packages). Note that miniconda still uses `conda` as the command.

::: {.column-margin}
pip is another package-management option — really not that different from conda. If you have reason to go that way, do it; plenty of tutorials around.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Also worth installing
[Seaborn](https://seaborn.pydata.org/examples/index.html) sits on top of matplotlib and is beautiful. SciPy is a deep toolbox of numerical routines — and unlike some later courses that make you build tools from fundamentals, *nothing in this course forbids it*: our concern is whether you can specify and verify, not whether you hand-rolled the algorithm. For the ML-taster Side Quest, [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) is what we'll reach for.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Python "environments" (optional reading)
Serious programmers give each project its own isolated "environment" with its own package versions, because packages sometimes conflict (the classic: some ML libraries lag behind the newest NumPy). For this course, working entirely in the base environment is fine. If you want the habit early: `conda create --name mcen1030`, then `conda activate mcen1030`, then `conda install numpy` installs into just that environment. Note you install per-environment — three environments can mean NumPy installed three times, and that's normal.
:::

## Level 2: MATLAB (week 11 and beyond)

MATLAB is the easiest install of everything on this page. As a CU student you have free access: create a MathWorks account with your CU email — instructions are [here](https://oit.colorado.edu/software-hardware/software-catalog/matlab), under the student "How to get it."

Once your account is tied to the school's license, you can install desktop MATLAB **or** use [MATLAB Online](https://matlab.mathworks.com) in the browser — students have used both, and you can hop back and forth. I like the immediacy of a local install and it runs a bit faster; Online gives you your code from any computer. For this course's purposes (week 11's translation work and HW 9), **MATLAB Online is entirely sufficient** — treat it as MATLAB's Colab.

Basic MATLAB is all this course needs; no toolboxes required. If you're going on in the department, toolboxes like Simulink (used in System Dynamics) can be added anytime, so there's no need to decide now.

The MathWorks "**MATLAB Onramp**" tutorial — find it under Online Training at [matlab.mathworks.com](https://matlab.mathworks.com) — is genuinely good, takes about two hours, and is the recommended pre-read for week 11 if you want a head start.

## Which level do I need, and when?

Weeks 1–10: **Level 0 is enough**, full stop — and the lesson pages themselves run Python in your browser for quick experiments, which is Level −1. The project (weeks 11–14): Level 0 still works, but Level 1 makes multi-file work and file management dramatically saner, and teams that take the Git Side Quest will want it. Week 11 / HW 9: **Level 2**, and MATLAB Online is fine. If your machine fights you at any point: bring it to a Monday session — installation archaeology is a group sport.
